solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What the blessed may get — some model children (6)

blocks.note: the Model T, Ford's famous car
issue = offspring, a legal word for children

annotation.surface: A fashion shoot, and what the children of the model world are blessed with.
annotation.walkthrough: The blessing is the one said after a sneeze: someone who hears 'bless you' may well be handed a tissue.
annotation.definitionFit: A sneezer, blessed by those nearby, is likely to need a tissue.

clue.text: I can do inane dances in a wet patch of earth (6,5)

indicators.note: the letters dance into new positions

annotation.surface: Someone boasts they can do silly dances in a puddle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A wet patch of earth' sounds like a muddy puddle, but it is a whole ocean covering part of the Earth.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the ocean is pictured modestly as a damp patch on the globe's surface.

clue.text: Family member taking on a large Barnet business? (5)

indicators.note: the outer word takes the letters on board, inside it

blocks.note: a son is a family member

annotation.surface: A son takes over a big business in Barnet, a north London borough.
annotation.walkthrough: Barnet is a London borough, but in rhyming slang 'Barnet Fair' means hair, so a Barnet business is a hair salon.
annotation.definitionFit: A salon is a hairdresser's, a business dealing in hair.

clue.text: Going out snorting whiff of cocaine is stimulating (8)

indicators.note: the outer word snorts, taking the letter in
a whiff is just a trace, the first letter

annotation.surface: A night out spent snorting cocaine is described as a thrill.
annotation.walkthrough: The drug picture is all surface: only the first letter of cocaine is used.
annotation.definitionFit: Something exciting stimulates the senses.

clue.text: Cloth rep ruined this woman in Bow, I heard (6)

indicators.note: the speaker is reporting a sound, not a spelling
Bow is in London's East End, where the Cockney accent drops the H of 'her'

blocks.note: her, with the H dropped Cockney-style

blocks.clueFragment: ruined this woman in Bow, I heard
blocks.note: the whole phrase spoken in a Cockney accent

annotation.surface: A cloth salesman has ruined a woman in the East End, so the gossip goes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cloth' is not fabric but the cloth, meaning the clergy; a rector represents it. Bow is an East End district where the Cockney accent drops initial H.
annotation.definitionFit: A rector is a parish priest, a man of the cloth.

clue.text: Standard Downing Street stocktake (6)

indicators.note: downing is swallowing, so the outer word takes the letters in

annotation.surface: A routine stocktake carried out at Downing Street, home of the Prime Minister.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Downing Street' looks like one name, but 'Downing' means swallowing. Stocktake is split as stock-take: to take livestock, which is what rustlers do.
annotation.definitionFit: To rustle is to steal livestock, literally to take stock.

clue.text: Material in my work upset official, perhaps (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsetting turns the word upside down, so it reads upwards

blocks.note: cor! = my! as an exclamation of surprise
official, as in the real or genuine one

annotation.surface: An official is upset by some material in a piece of the speaker's work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation here, not a possessive; 'cor' is the British equivalent.
annotation.definitionFit: Corporeal means physical, having a material body.

clue.text: Upper-class sort going topless is not on (3)

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, which goes

blocks.note: a toff is a posh person

annotation.surface: A posh person taking their top off is told that is not acceptable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not on' is British for unacceptable, which fits the surface, but it also simply means off.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'not on' can mean switched off or cancelled, as well as the British sense of unacceptable.

clue.text: Unregulated bond-holders wild about a Republican (2,5,6)

indicators.note: the letters run wild into a new order
the anagram goes around the other letters

annotation.surface: Unregulated bondholders are furious about a Republican.
annotation.walkthrough: The rearranged BONDHOLDERS wraps around A R, which sits between the B and the RED.
annotation.definitionFit: A no-holds-barred fight has no rules restricting it.

clue.text: Is clue I do askew or very pleasing to you? (9)

indicators.note: askew means out of line, so the letters are knocked out of order

annotation.surface: The setter asks the solver whether this clue is crooked or a treat.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue talks about itself, inviting the solver to judge it, while its first four words are the letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Something delicious is highly pleasing to the one enjoying it.

clue.text: Load of work abandoned by head of government (4)

indicators.note: the letter walks away from the word, leaving it
the head of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: A government leader walks away from a heavy workload.
annotation.walkthrough: Graft is British slang for hard work. A raft of something is a large amount of it.
annotation.definitionFit: A raft of things, like a load of them, is a large number.

clue.text: Attractive sort of old lady … good catch (6)

annotation.surface: An appealing old lady is described as a real catch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Attractive' reads as good-looking, but here it means literally pulling things towards it.
annotation.definitionFit: A magnet attracts metal, so it is quite literally an attractive sort of thing.

clue.text: One observing old knight striking person (8)

blocks.note: a looker is a strikingly attractive person

annotation.surface: Someone watches an old knight hit another person.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Striking' suggests a blow, but a striking person is simply good-looking.
annotation.definitionFit: An onlooker is someone who watches without taking part.

clue.text: Gutted after kicking dearest vice (11)

indicators.note: the letters are kicked about into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone is devastated after giving up their favourite bad habit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' is British slang for bitterly disappointed, which the surface uses, but it also means disembowelled.
annotation.definitionFit: To eviscerate is to remove the guts, so eviscerated means gutted.

clue.text: Limited company with new penalty by Democrat (8)

annotation.surface: A limited company is handed a new penalty alongside a Democrat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Limited company' reads as one business term (Ltd), but 'Limited' is the definition and 'company' starts the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Confined means restricted, kept within limits.

clue.text: Company men bringing in a bit of trade for Sky (9)

indicators.note: the company men bring the A in between them
a bit of a word here is its first letter

annotation.surface: Company staff bring in some business for Sky, the British broadcaster.
annotation.walkthrough: Sky reads as the TV company, which suits the business picture, but it is just the heavens.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though a poetic one: firmament is an old word for the heavens above.

clue.text: Having gone the wrong way, be morally corrupt (4)

indicators.note: going the wrong way means running backwards

blocks.note: to be is to live, exist

annotation.surface: Someone who has strayed from the path is told they are corrupt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gone the wrong way' sounds moral, which suits the surface, but it simply reverses the word next to it.
annotation.definitionFit: Evil means wicked, morally bad.

clue.text: European schoolboy gains foremost of scholarships (8)

indicators.note: the outer word gains the letter inside it
the foremost letter is the first

blocks.note: an Etonian is a pupil at Eton College

annotation.surface: A European schoolboy wins a top scholarship.
annotation.walkthrough: Eton is England's best-known private boarding school, so an Etonian is the standard crossword schoolboy.
annotation.definitionFit: An Estonian comes from Estonia, a European country.

clue.text: Lawyers to welcome key Russian representative (4)

indicators.note: the outer word takes the inner letter in, as a host welcomes a guest

blocks.note: the Bar = barristers as a body

annotation.walkthrough: The bear is the national symbol of Russia, so it represents the country as a lion does England.
annotation.surface: Lawyers prepare to receive an important Russian envoy.
annotation.definitionFit: The bear is Russia's traditional emblem, so it stands for the country.

clue.text: Church in Calais I renovated with bishop (8)

indicators.note: renovating rebuilds something, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

annotation.surface: A church in Calais is restored with the help of a bishop.
annotation.walkthrough: The bishop's B goes at the front even though 'with bishop' ends the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a basilica is one particular kind of church, often given special status by the Pope.

clue.text: Help to turn around a crap keeper in America (6)

indicators.note: the word turns round and runs backwards

blocks.note: a = per, as in ten pounds a head

annotation.surface: Someone is asked to help turn round a hopeless goalkeeper in the US.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A crap keeper' reads as a poor goalkeeper, but it is something that keeps crap in: diaper is the American word for a nappy.
annotation.definitionFit: Americans call a baby's nappy a diaper, which contains its mess.

clue.text: US trainer admitting bit of ice is extra-slippery (8)

indicators.note: the outer word lets the letter in
a bit of a word here is its first letter

blocks.note: sneaker is the American word for a trainer, a sports shoe

annotation.surface: An American sports coach concedes that ice has made the ground more slippery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trainer' reads as a coach, but in Britain a trainer is a running shoe, which Americans call a sneaker.
annotation.definitionFit: Sneakier means more sly and evasive, harder to pin down.

clue.text: Men reversing cherry-hued Sierra and Fiats (6)

indicators.note: the word after it runs backwards

blocks.note: OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
Sierra is S in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Some men are backing red Ford Sierras and Fiat cars.
annotation.walkthrough: Sierra and Fiat look like car makes, but a fiat is a decree and Sierra is just the letter S.
annotation.definitionFit: A fiat is an authoritative order.

clue.text: Ideal way to get up with energy in the morning (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means reading upwards

annotation.surface: The perfect way to get out of bed full of energy in the morning.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is advice on waking, and a dream is exactly what you leave behind when you get up.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used as an adjective: a perfect partner can be called a dream as well as ideal.

clue.text: Track one and two released by the Sweet (4)

indicators.note: letters one and two are let go from the word

blocks.note: a cut is a track on an album
THE without its first two letters

annotation.surface: A track is released by the 1970s glam-rock band The Sweet.
annotation.walkthrough: The Sweet were a real British glam-rock band, but the capital S only disguises the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Cute means sweet, charmingly attractive.

clue.text: Exercise in American English (3)

annotation.surface: A gym session, or perhaps a language drill in American English.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Exercise' is a verb here: to exercise a right is to use it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: exercising a right or a skill means putting it to work.

clue.text: Quiet type based for a long time in Lincoln? (9)

definitions.note: Lincoln is one example of a president, hence the question mark

blocks.clueFragment: type based for a long time
blocks.note: a resident lives in a place long-term

annotation.surface: A quiet person who has lived in the English city of Lincoln for years.
annotation.walkthrough: Lincoln reads as the English cathedral city, but it is Abraham Lincoln, the US president.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Abraham Lincoln held the office, so he stands for its holders, flagged by the question mark.

clue.text: 100 per cent of B and A, perhaps, but not L (6)

indicators.note: the named letter is left out

blocks.note: A is an example of a letter

annotation.surface: It reads like a quiz about letters: all of B and A, except L.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue looks like a sum of letters, but '100 per cent' is the definition: fully recovered from an illness.
annotation.definitionFit: Feeling 100 per cent after illness is being fully better.

clue.text: Numbers broken into by wildly keen Drifters? (6)

indicators.note: the outer word is burgled, the inner word getting inside it

annotation.surface: Wildly keen fans of the soul group The Drifters break into the charts.
annotation.walkthrough: The Drifters were an American vocal group, which the capital D exploits; here they are wanderers.
annotation.definitionFit: Nomads drift from place to place with no fixed home.
